catalog_quote: Since Mathevet did not mark stress, we must turn to other sources, one external and one internal, to determine the stress pattern of Nipmuck. The PA Alternating Stress Rule provides the external source, and a basis from which to begin the analysis of Nipmuck. In PA, every long vowel, and every other short vowel (starting from the left of the word) receives stress (Aubin 1980). For the most part, Ojibwe retains this stress pattern, as in the following examples, in which the stressed vowels are underlined: *masenahikanali > Oj. mazina?iganan 'books' ... In the first word, every other vowel is stressed in both Ojibwe and PA, since all the vowels are short. In the second word, every long vowel and every short vowel (starting at the beginning of the word, and then restarting after a long vowel) is stressed. ... new_statements.quote: Since Mathevet did not mark stress, we must turn to other sources, one external and one internal, to determine the stress pattern of Nipmuck. The PA Alternating Stress Rule provides the external source, and a basis from which to begin the analysis of Nipmuck. In PA, every long vowel, and every other short vowel (starting from the left of the word) receives stress (Aubin 1980). new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Nipmuck has an empty rule. This work supplies a rule (PA-type alternating, length-sensitive stress), explicitly hedged as inferred ('seems', 'seemingly identical to that of PA') because the manuscript does not mark stress. Refines rather than contradicts, since there is no prior placement to disagree with.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not recorded in the only primary source (Mathevet's manuscript). Gustafson infers, from vowel syncope patterns, that Nipmuck kept the Proto-Algonquian Alternating Stress Rule: every long vowel is stressed, and among short vowels every other one counting from the left of the word is stressed, the count restarting after each long vowel (i.e. left-to-right iterative alternation sensitive to vowel length). This is a reconstruction from indirect evidence, not an observation.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the alternating pattern assigns stress to multiple syllables per word (every long vowel and every other short vowel) with no primary/secondary distinction stated.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. The inference rests on two syncope examples (loss of an unstressed short vowel) plus an Abenaki-like initial-syllable syncope (p. 38); p. 35 cites Goddard (1981) that stressed syllables are exempt from final-syllable loss in Massachusett, which the thesis applies partly to Nipmuck.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works concern the language of Father Mathevet's 18th-century 'Mots loups' manuscript (Loup A), which Gustafson identifies as Nipmuck; the thesis is a philological grammar of that single manuscript, and Day 1975 is its edition. No living-speaker data exist, so any stress statement is a reconstruction.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim on printed p. 37 of the thesis PDF we hold (page image opened). The deciding source is the only grammar of the language and is. but the stress statement itself is a comparative inference (PA Alternating Stress Rule projected onto an 18th-c. manuscript that marks no stress, supported by syncope), so the record can never be better than hedged -- 'thin' by nature of the evidence, not by neglect, and the existing weight-sensitive (tentative) / weight-hedged coding already reflects that. The two open specialist papers downloaded now (Costa 2007, Goddard 2016) are silent on a Loup stress rule; Costa's remarks on metrically conditioned syncope in SNEA are compatible with Gustafson. One caution worth carrying in the record's idn/caution field (not a reclassify): Goddard 2016 argues the Loup A manuscript mixes three distinct SNEA varieties (Loup 1-3), so 'Nipmuck' as a single-language label for M

sources.quote: No Loup stress rule. 'Abenaki Syncope is only sporadic in Loup and Narragansett' (p. 98); conditioning of syncope in SNEA 'seems to depend on currently ill-understood metrical factors' (fn. 72); in Massachusett syncope is triggered 'when the syllable in question is odd numbered or follows a long vowel' (p. 98).
